scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that leans toward required breadth while granting the value of job preparation; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Universities must decide whether to broaden their students or to train them for specific jobs.
Some believe universities should require students to take courses outside their field, while others believe they should only require courses that prepare students for jobs.
I lean toward requiring some breadth, but I accept that job preparation also deserves real weight.
First, studying outside one's field makes students wiser and more complete thinkers.
Courses in other subjects expose students to new ideas and ways of seeing the world.
For example, an engineering student who studies ethics may use her skills more responsibly.
This shows that breadth can produce thoughtful citizens, not merely trained workers.
Such variety also builds flexible skills, like reasoning and writing, useful in any career.
Many students discover unexpected interests through subjects they would never have chosen alone.
For these reasons, I believe some required breadth is valuable.
Second, however, the opposing view rightly values courses that prepare students for work.
Students need jobs after graduating, and useful training helps them build secure lives.
Consider a student deep in debt who urgently needs practical skills to find employment soon.
Such cases show that job preparation is not selfish but a genuine and pressing need.
Too many unrelated courses can also crowd out the deep training a career demands.
A wise university balances broad learning with the practical skills students will rely on.
Both views, then, point to needs that a good education must somehow combine.
In conclusion, I believe universities should require some study beyond a student's own field.
But preparing students for work also matters and should not be ignored.
The wisest universities give students broad horizons while still building the skills their careers require.
